summary:
Nevada stands under the United States federal framework, which governs passports, entry screening, federal custody and federal care measures; those apply within the state and are carried by the national record. The findings below are specific to Nevada.

A national legal risk assessment published in July 2026 places Nevada in its Low-Risk group, directly below the most-protective tier and alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia. The assessment credits Nevada with fairly robust non-discrimination policies while finding that it falls short on healthcare equity and on protections for incarcerated transgender people.

Nevada prohibits discrimination based on gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public accommodation under laws effective 1 October 2011, extended throughout state statutes effective 1 July 2017. In November 2022 voters approved Question 1 by 58 per cent, adding sexual orientation and gender identity or expression to the state Constitution's equal protection clause.

The state hate-crime law provides additional penalties for crimes motivated by actual or perceived characteristics; gender identity or expression was added by legislation passed in May 2013 and effective 1 October 2013, and a hate-crime reporting hotline was established in January 2025.

State identity documents are among Nevada's clearest divergences from federal practice. Since 2016 Nevada Vital Records issues a corrected-gender birth certificate on receipt of two affidavits reflecting preferred gender, with sex reassignment surgery not required, and comparable changes are available for driver's licences and state IDs. The DMV and Vital Records offer an X third-gender designation on driver's licences, birth certificates and state IDs with no medical documentation required, in place since 2019. Legislation signed 22 June 2017 abolished the 1988 requirement that transgender people publish their names in newspapers before legal sex changes on government documents.

Healthcare access is protected by state law. The state Medicaid agency announced in March 2018 that it would cover sex-reassignment surgery, following a 22 June 2017 veto of a coverage mandate, and state law bans health insurers from discriminating against transgender patients. A bill passed in June 2023 and signed by the governor requires health insurers, including Medicaid, to cover all medically necessary gender-affirming treatments, effective 1 January 2024. The governor separately vetoed the 2023 omnibus bill SB 302, which would have shielded gender-affirming care and mandated Medicaid surgery coverage.

In May 2023 the governor signed legislation explicitly protecting transgender and intersex individuals in state correctional facilities, which sits against the July 2026 assessment's finding that protections for incarcerated transgender people remain a shortfall.

School sport is the sharpest documented restriction. In April 2025 the Nevada Interscholastic Activities Association reversed its 2016 policy and now requires transgender athletes to compete under their sex assigned at birth. A governor-supported 2026 ballot initiative that would generally determine school sports eligibility by sex assigned at birth failed to reach the November 2026 ballot.

Relationship recognition is settled in Nevada. Same-sex marriage became legal on 8 October 2014 when the Ninth Circuit struck down the state's ban in Sevcik v. Sandoval, the marriage statute incorporated gender-neutral language effective 1 July 2017, voters removed the constitutional ban by approving Question 2 with 62 per cent in November 2020, and the Nevada Supreme Court ordered retroactive recognition in December 2020 of out-of-state same-sex marriages performed before 2014. The Nevada Domestic Partnership Act, effective 1 October 2009 after a veto override, grants many marriage rights but exempts employers from providing medical coverage to domestic partners and leaves parental rights less clearly defined, with uncertain recognition between states.
tangentialFactors:
The July 2026 assessment groups Nevada with eight other jurisdictions in a single Low-Risk tier rather than treating it as an outlier; the grouping places Nevada below the most-protective tier, so the state's profile is one of broad statutory protection with identified gaps rather than a leading position.

The Movement Advancement Project's Equality Map is the comparison source used to situate Nevada among state-by-state rules on whether transgender people may use public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity. The inventory does not state Nevada's specific entry on that map.

Nevada's trajectory has not been uniformly protective. The governor's June 2017 veto of a Medicaid surgery coverage mandate and his veto of the 2023 SB 302 omnibus show that legislative gains have been narrowed at the executive stage, while the April 2025 reversal by the Nevada Interscholastic Activities Association shows a state body moving toward restriction in the same period that the state's document and healthcare rules moved the other way.

The failure of the 2026 school-sports ballot initiative to qualify for the November 2026 ballot leaves the birth-sex eligibility rule adopted by the interscholastic association in April 2025 as the operative standard for school sport, without a statewide statutory codification.
localsOnly:
Legal sex change on Nevada government documents requires no surgery and no publication: since 2016 Vital Records issues a corrected-gender birth certificate on two affidavits alone, driver's licences and state IDs follow the same route, and the 2017 legislation signed 22 June 2017 removed the 1988 newspaper publication requirement. An X third-gender designation is available on driver's licences, birth certificates and state IDs without medical documentation.

Residents have statutory coverage across employment, housing and public accommodation on gender identity or expression since 2011, extended statewide in 2017 and entrenched in the state Constitution's equal protection clause by the 58 per cent vote on Question 1 in November 2022. Gender identity or expression has been a hate-crime ground since 1 October 2013, with a state reporting hotline operating since January 2025.

Residents under 18 are covered by a conversion therapy ban signed 17 May 2017 and effective 1 January 2018, and by the anti-bullying statute SB 504, effective 1 July 2015, which expressly lists gender identity or expression as a protected ground and directs school policies, reporting, parent notification and staff training.

Transgender and intersex people in state correctional facilities are explicitly protected under legislation approved by the governor in May 2023. The gay panic defence was repealed by legislation signed 14 May 2019, effective 1 October 2019.

Residents obtain gender-affirming care through insurers barred by state law from discriminating against transgender patients, Medicaid coverage of sex-reassignment surgery in place since March 2018, and the June 2023 mandate covering all medically necessary gender-affirming treatments from 1 January 2024.

Nevada's Domestic Partnership Act, effective 1 October 2009, grants many marriage rights while exempting private and public employers from providing medical coverage to domestic partners and leaving parental rights less well defined, with uncertain recognition in other states.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory cites the Movement Advancement Project's Equality Map as the source situating Nevada on public bathroom and facilities rules, but does not record Nevada's specific entry; whether Nevada restricts facilities access by gender identity is unresolved on this evidence.

No Nevada-specific incident data on violence against transgender people, and no dated account of any such incident, appears in the inventory, so no prevalence claim about violence in the state can be sourced here. The July 2026 assessment's methodology, its measurement window and its criteria for the Low-Risk tier are not stated in the inventory.

How the federal document, entry and custody measures interact with Nevada's state-issued identity documents and state correctional protections is not addressed by the sources; the inventory records the two layers separately.

Whether the April 2025 interscholastic eligibility rule has been challenged in Nevada courts, and whether any state agency has issued guidance on facilities access for transgender visitors, are not sourced.
